set.statement: In general-population cohorts followed over time and in first-episode case-control studies, people who use cannabis, compared with people who do not, are more likely to develop psychotic symptoms or a psychotic disorder, and the association is stronger with more frequent use. Few sources give absolute risks. As a base rate, 362 of 50,087 men conscripted in Sweden in 1969 (about 7 in 1,000, editors' calculation) were diagnosed with schizophrenia by about age 45, whatever their cannabis use (as tabulated in a narrative review, Gage et al., 2016); in the same cohort, as tabulated in a meta-analysis, 215 of 36,429 men who had never used cannabis by conscription (about 6 in 1,000) and 28 of 731 who had used it more than 50 times (about 38 in 1,000) were later admitted to hospital with schizophrenia, crude proportions with nothing adjusted (editors' calculation; Marconi et al., 2016). A systematic review of seven cohorts published to 2006 (Moore et al., 2007; AMSTAR 2 low confidence) pooled each cohort's own adjusted odds ratio (about 60 confounders across the studies, among them other substance use, personality traits, intellectual ability and other mental health problems): 1.41 (95% CI 1.20 to 1.65; I² 19%) for any later psychotic outcome, mostly self-reported or interview-rated symptoms, after ever use (past-year use in one cohort) against never use; 2.09 (1.54 to 2.84; I² 44%) for each cohort's most frequent use (from more than 50 lifetime occasions to weekly or daily use or dependence) against no use, three of the six estimates not adjusted for other drug use; and 2.58 (1.08 to 6.13; I² 67%) for a psychotic disorder after ever use in the three cohorts with that outcome, or 1.82 (1.01 to 3.30) without the most heterogeneous one. Across the seven cohorts, adjustment removed on average about 45% of the crude excess odds (10% to 80% by cohort, for exposure contrasts the review does not state). Of three cohorts published after that review, as summarized by Gage et al. (2016), the association did not remain after adjustment in two (Zurich; ALSPAC, 1.12, 0.76 to 1.65, after adjustment for tobacco and other illicit drugs, an adjustment the original authors discussed as possible over-adjustment, the association having remained after adjustment for pre-birth and childhood factors), while a Californian hospital cohort reported a hazard ratio of 8.16 (5.08 to 13.12) for later admission with schizophrenia after a hospital diagnosis of cannabis use disorder, against people admitted with appendicitis. A meta-analysis of crude counts from ten studies (Marconi et al., 2016; AMSTAR 2 critically low) found the odds of a psychosis-related outcome rising with rank on each study's own scale of use: a fitted odds ratio of 3.90 (2.84 to 5.34; I² 82%) for the single most-exposed person on each scale and 3.40 (2.55 to 4.54) for the middle of the top fifth, against no use (never use in most studies, no use in the past year or at a given age in some), with nothing adjusted and with category-level odds that did not rise steadily in several studies; five of its six cohorts are reports the 2007 review also pooled. In two first-episode case-control studies from one team, daily use as the person's most consistent pattern over the lifetime was reported more often by people with a psychotic disorder than by controls: fully adjusted odds ratio 3.2 (2.2 to 4.1) against never or occasional use (901 cases and 1,237 population controls at 11 sites in Europe and Brazil; adjusted for age, gender, ethnicity, education, employment, tobacco and other drugs; Di Forti et al., 2019) and 3.04 against never use (410 inpatients and 370 controls recruited by advertisement in south London; adjusted also for alcohol; Di Forti et al., 2015), whereas occasional use was not associated (0.84 and 0.96 for low- and high-potency types at the 11 sites; 0.58 for less-than-weekly use in south London), ever use only weakly (1.3, 1.1 to 1.6) or not at all (0.93), and current use at the 11 sites not after full adjustment (1.1, 0.9 to 1.5). Whether starting young adds risk beyond the amount used was not shown: the cohort review found no robust evidence that it does (Moore et al., 2007), and at the 11 sites first use at 15 or younger had a fully adjusted odds ratio of 1.6 (1.1 to 2.1) against never use while the daily-use estimate changed little (3.1) when age at first use was added. Other absolute figures in the reviews are statements or calculations rather than measurements: the 2007 review puts lifetime risk of chronic psychotic disorders with regular use below 3% without showing how (Moore et al., 2007); Hall (2015) gives as its best estimate a doubling from about 7 to 14 in 1,000 with regular use, which applies the relative estimate to a base rate as if it were causal; and Gage et al. (2016) give a lifetime risk of schizophrenia of about 2% with regular use if the association is causal. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
set.plain: In studies that followed young people for years, those who had used cannabis were more likely to have psychotic symptoms or a psychotic illness later than those who had not, and the link was stronger for those who used it most often, such as daily. In a large Swedish study, about 7 in 1,000 men were diagnosed with schizophrenia by about age 45, whatever their cannabis use. In the same study, about 6 in 1,000 men who had never used cannabis and about 38 in 1,000 who had used it more than 50 times later went to hospital with schizophrenia, before other differences between them were taken into account. In two studies of people with a first episode of psychosis, using cannabis only now and then was not linked to psychosis. Part of the link shrank when other differences between people were taken into account, and these studies cannot show that cannabis caused it.
set.magnitude: Moore et al. 2007 (7 cohorts; random-effects pooling of each cohort's adjusted odds ratio): any psychotic outcome, ever vs never use, 1.41 (1.20–1.65), I² 19.2%; most frequent use vs none, 2.09 (1.54–2.84), I² 44.1% (1.92, 1.50–2.47, without NEMESIS); psychotic disorder, ever use, 3 cohorts, 2.58 (1.08–6.13), I² 66.9% (1.82, 1.01–3.30, without NEMESIS); adjustment attenuated crude estimates by about 45% on average (10% to 80%; exposure contrast per cohort not stated). Later cohorts as summarized by Gage et al. 2016: ALSPAC 1.12 (0.76–1.65) after full adjustment; Zurich lost after adjustment; California HR 8.16 (5.08–13.12). Marconi et al. 2016 (10 studies, 66,816 people, crude counts): fitted OR 3.90 (2.84–5.34) for the most-exposed rank vs no use, I² 82%; 3.40 (2.55–4.54) for the median of the top 20%; 1.97 (1.68–2.31) for the median person who had used. Di Forti et al. 2019 (901 cases, 1,237 controls; fully adjusted): daily use vs never or occasional 3.2 (2.2–4.1); more than once a week 1.4 (1.0–2.0); occasional use vs never 0.84 (low potency) and 0.96 (high potency); ever use 1.3 (1.1–1.6); current use 1.1 (0.9–1.5); first use at 15 or younger vs never 1.6 (1.1–2.1). Di Forti et al. 2015 (410 cases, 370 controls; adjusted): every day 3.04 (printed 1.91–7.76), weekends 1.04, less than weekly 0.58 (0.25–1.32), ever use 0.93 (0.67–1.52). Absolute: Swedish conscripts, 362 of 50,087 diagnosed with schizophrenia by about age 45, about 7 in 1,000 (editors' calculation; all levels of use); crude, admission with schizophrenia, 215 of 36,429 with no use (about 6 in 1,000) and 28 of 731 with more than 50 occasions (about 38 in 1,000) (editors' calculation from Marconi et al.'s Table 1; unadjusted). Statements and illustrations: lifetime risk of chronic psychotic disorder with regular use below 3%, no derivation (Moore et al., 2007); 7 rising to 14 in 1,000 with regular use, applying a doubling (Hall, 2015); about 2% lifetime risk with regular use if causal (Gage et al., 2016).
set.comparator: People in the same cohorts who had never used cannabis or did not use it (in the crude meta-analysis, no use meant never use in most studies but no use in the past year or at a given age in some); in the case-control studies, controls without psychosis, with never use, or never or only occasional use, as the reference group stated
set.grade.domains.publication_bias.note: Egger tests in both meta-analyses found no small-study signal, each with little power (cards sc_moore_2007 and sc_marconi_2016); not rated down.
set.grade.reasoning: Observational, starts low; down one for risk of bias: very low. Rated as worded, an association; whether it is causal is the separate, contested question (see the answer on whether cannabis causes psychosis). Status replicated: several independent cohorts point the same way (CHDS, Dunedin, ECA, EDSP and the Swedish conscripts), and daily use is associated in both case-control studies. Overlapping sources are counted once: five of the six cohorts in the crude meta-analysis are reports that Moore et al. pooled, and its London case-control data are the sample of Di Forti et al. (2015); Gage et al. (2016) restate Moore et al.'s pooled figures, and their informal re-pooling with two later cohorts is not used because it cannot be reproduced from the estimates the review prints (card sc_gage_2016); Hall (2015) restates Moore et al.'s figures. The only absolute risks by level of use are crude proportions from one cohort; the other absolute figures in the reviews are statements or conditional calculations, not measurements.

set.statement: In two case-control studies from one research team, people presenting with a first episode of psychosis, compared with controls from the same areas, more often reported using high-potency types of cannabis, and the largest odds ratios were for daily use of high-potency types; low-potency types, taken over all frequencies of use, were not associated with psychosis after adjustment, although at the 11 sites daily use of low-potency types was; potency was assigned from the type of cannabis people named, not measured. In south London (410 inpatients aged 18 to 65 with first-episode psychosis, 2005 to 2011, and 370 controls recruited by advertisement; Di Forti et al., 2015), 53% of patients and 19% of controls said they had mostly used skunk-like cannabis, and 14% and 44% hash-like cannabis; against people who had never used cannabis, adjusted odds ratios (for age, gender, ethnic origin, tobacco, alcohol, other drugs, education and employment) were 2.91 (printed 95% CI 1.52 to 3.60) for mainly skunk-like use and 0.83 (0.52 to 1.77) for mainly hash-like use, and 5.40 (2.80 to 11.30) for daily skunk-like use against 0.91 for daily hash-like use; several printed intervals do not fit their estimates or p-values, and the controls' exposure is printed in two versions that cannot both be right. At 11 sites in the UK, the Netherlands, France, Spain, Italy and Brazil (901 people with first-episode psychosis and 1,237 population controls, 2010 to 2015; Di Forti et al., 2019), where a type counted as high potency if European and national figures put its mean THC at 10% or more, 37.1% of cases and 19.4% of controls had used types classed as high potency; fully adjusted odds ratios against never use (for age, gender, ethnicity, education, employment, tobacco and other drugs) were 1.6 (1.2 to 2.2) for use of high-potency types and 1.1 (0.9 to 1.5) for use of low-potency types, 1.5 (1.1 to 2.6) for high-potency use after also adjusting for daily use, and 4.78 (2.5 to 6.3) for daily use of high-potency types against 2.19 (1.4 to 3.6) for daily use of low-potency types, while occasional use of either kind was not associated (0.96 and 0.84); the two daily intervals overlap and there was no evidence that the association with frequency differed by type (interaction p = 0.25), so a larger risk with daily high-potency than with daily low-potency use is not statistically shown; site estimates for high-potency use against never use ranged from 0.6 to 3.6 without significant variation between sites. Both studies recorded cannabis type from recall after the illness began, measured no THC or cannabidiol and share investigators (the 2019 paper presents its daily high-potency finding as a replication of the 2015 study), and both give attributable fractions for high-potency use (24% and 12.2%) that assume the associations are causal; the 24% cannot be reproduced from its printed inputs. A narrative review from the same group reports that the team's own correspondence reply found no evidence that people using high-potency cannabis were more genetically predisposed to psychosis, judged by schizophrenia polygenic scores, without giving figures (Murray et al., 2016), whereas another review judged it too early to assume that only high-potency cannabis carries risk, because studies from before it was widespread also found an association, and asked that people selecting the extremes of use for other reasons be considered (Gage et al., 2016); the cohorts pooled to 2006 recorded how often people used, not what they used (Moore et al., 2007). Certainty: very low. Status: replicated by the same team.
set.plain: Two studies by one team compared people who had a first episode of psychosis with people from the same areas who had not. People with psychosis more often said they had used strong types of cannabis. The strongest link was with using strong types every day: about 5 times the odds of psychosis compared with never using. Daily use of weaker types went with about 2 times the odds; the gap between these two could be due to chance. Using any type only now and then was not linked to psychosis, and nor was using weaker types once all patterns of use were counted together. Nobody measured the strength of the cannabis people actually used: it was guessed from the type they named, after they became ill. These studies cannot show that strong cannabis caused the psychosis.
set.magnitude: Di Forti et al. 2015 (410 cases, 370 controls; adjusted): mainly skunk-like 2.91 (1.52–3.60 as printed), mainly hash-like 0.83 (0.52–1.77); daily skunk-like 5.40 (2.80–11.30), at weekends 2.70, less than weekly 1.90; daily hash-like 0.91, at weekends 0.62, less than weekly 0.49; mainly skunk-like use in 53% of patients and 19% of controls. Di Forti et al. 2019 (901 cases, 1,237 controls; fully adjusted, against never use): high-potency types 1.6 (1.2–2.2), 1.5 (1.1–2.6) also adjusted for daily use; low-potency types 1.1 (0.9–1.5); daily high potency 4.78 (2.5–6.3), daily low potency 2.19 (1.4–3.6), frequency-by-type interaction p = 0.25; more than weekly 1.57 and 1.36, occasional 0.96 and 0.84; high-potency use in 37.1% of cases and 19.4% of controls; site-specific high-potency odds ratios 0.6 to 3.6 (variation by site p = 0.45). Attributable fractions assuming causality: high-potency use 24.0% (not reproducible from its inputs) and 12.2% (3.0–16.1).
set.exposure: Type of cannabis, as recalled and named by participants: in south London the type mostly used, skunk-like (high potency) or hash-like (low potency), grouped by police seizure data; at the 11 sites, lifetime use by potency class of the type named, high (mean THC of 10% or more for that type in European and national figures) or low; and these combined with the lifetime frequency of the most consistent pattern of use
set.grade.domains.indirectness.note: Potency was not measured: it was assigned from the type name, using police seizure data in south London or European and national figures for mean THC by type at the 11 sites (dichotomized at 10%), without cannabidiol; what any person actually used is unknown.
set.grade.domains.imprecision.note: The contrast the claim is about, between potency types, is imprecise: at the 11 sites the overall high- and low-potency intervals overlap (1.2 to 2.2; 0.9 to 1.5), the two daily intervals overlap (2.5 to 6.3; 1.4 to 3.6) and the association with frequency did not differ significantly by type (interaction p = 0.25); several printed intervals in both studies do not fit their estimates.
set.grade.reasoning: Observational, starts low; down one each for risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision, which is below the floor: very low. The two studies share investigators and methods, and the 2019 paper presents its daily high-potency finding as a replication of the 2015 study, so they count as replication by the same team, not independent replication; the team's earlier south London reports and the London case-control data pooled by Marconi et al. (2016) are the same sample and add nothing independent. No general-population cohort read here measured potency.

evidence_set: The high-potency odds ratio did not vary significantly by site (p = 0.45): fully adjusted site estimates against never use from 3.6 (1.5 to 7.7) in Amsterdam to 0.6 (0.1 to 2.5) in Palermo; London 2.4 (1.4 to 4.0); Paris 2.1 (0.8 to 3.6).

evidence_add.extracted: 901 cases and 1,237 population controls at 11 sites, recruited between May 1, 2010, and April 1, 2015. Questions on the type of cannabis made no reference to potency; potency was assigned from THC concentrations by type in a 2016 European report, supplemented by national data. The main text speaks of lifetime use of cannabis by potency, not of the type mainly used: in Table 2 every person who had used is in one potency class (331 + 240 = 571 of 574 controls, potency missing for 3; 251 + 334 = 585 cases; editors' arithmetic). Against never use, fully adjusted (Figure 1): occasional use 0.84 (THC below 10%) and 0.96 (10% or more), use more than once a week 1.36 and 1.57, daily use 2.19 and 4.78, the text giving 2.2 (1.4 to 3.6) and 4.8 (2.5 to 6.3); no evidence of interaction between frequency of use and type (p = 0.25). The authors present the daily high-potency finding as a replication of their previous south London study (ref. 28, Di Forti et al., 2015).

set.statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether, or how much, cannabis use causes psychotic disorders such as schizophrenia. The association with later psychosis is consistent and stronger with frequent use (see the answer on how often people use), but in the studies read a substantial part of it shrinks when measured confounders are taken into account, and genetically informed studies suggest that a further part reflects shared family or genetic liability, or genetic liability to schizophrenia making cannabis use more likely; none of these designs excludes a causal contribution, and none measures the effect of daily or high-potency use (the genetic studies concern ever trying cannabis, the co-relative study cannabis misuse). Adjustment for each cohort's measured confounders removed on average about 45% (10% to 80%) of the crude excess odds in seven cohorts, for exposure contrasts the review does not state (Moore et al., 2007). In the one co-relative study, a Swedish national registry study (as Ksir & Hart, 2016, describe it) described in a viewpoint whose second author co-wrote it (Gillespie & Kendler, 2021), the odds ratio for schizophrenia with cannabis misuse fell from 10.44 in the general population to 5.07 in full siblings and to 3.52 (3.92 in the viewpoint's table) in identical twins discordant for misuse, with no significance test at the twin level and the adjustment set not stated; an earlier cross-sectional sibling-pair study, by contrast, is described as arguing against stable family confounding (Gage et al., 2016). Three two-sample Mendelian randomization studies used genetic variants for having ever used cannabis, which explain about 1% or less of the variation in ever use where this is reported and, in two of the studies, did not reach genome-wide significance, with no adjustment beyond the source studies in the main analyses. The odds ratio for schizophrenia by genetic liability to ever use was 1.04 (95% CI 1.01 to 1.07) per doubling of the odds of ever use, a smaller step than one unit of log odds, and 1.01 (0.93 to 1.10) by the pleiotropy-robust MR-Egger method (Gage et al., 2017); 1.08 (1.02 to 1.14) per unit of log odds, which its authors rescale to 1.37 for ever against never use (Vaucher et al., 2018); and, per unit of log odds, 1.04 (p = 0.81) with five genome-wide significant variants or 1.10 (0.99 to 1.21) with 69 variants below that threshold, whose inverse-variance and weighted-median estimates did not reach significance (p = 0.074 and 0.156) while the outlier-filtered GSMR estimate, with 74 variants, did (1.21, p = 0.017) (Pasman et al., 2018). In the reverse direction, genetic liability to schizophrenia was associated with ever using cannabis (1.10, 1.05 to 1.14, per doubling, Gage et al., 2017; 1.16, 1.06 to 1.27, per unit of log odds, Pasman et al., 2018), although the MR-Egger estimates in this direction were imprecise and included no effect (1.17, 0.96 to 1.43; 1.07, p = 0.81), and the genetic correlation between ever use and schizophrenia was 0.25 (Pasman et al., 2018, as corrected). These three studies share consortium data and are not independent, and their authors read them differently: one as strongly supporting a causal role of cannabis use (Vaucher et al., 2018), the other two as weak evidence in that direction and stronger evidence for the reverse (Gage et al., 2017; Pasman et al., 2018). The 2007 systematic review read its cohorts as consistent with an increased risk independent of the confounders measured and as enough to warn young people (Moore et al., 2007); later reviews and a viewpoint read the evidence available to them as shared vulnerability (Ksir & Hart, 2016), as partly causal with an appreciable non-causal share (Gillespie & Kendler, 2021), or as strong enough for public-health messages that cannabis can increase the risk (Gage et al., 2016; Murray et al., 2016, which calls cannabis a component cause). Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
set.plain: Does cannabis cause psychosis? This has not been shown either way. People who use cannabis, especially often, are more likely to develop psychosis, but about half of that link shrank, on average, once other differences between people were taken into account. In a Swedish study of relatives, the link got smaller the more closely related two people were, but it was still there between identical twins, though nobody checked whether that could be chance. Gene studies found that genes linked to schizophrenia go with a higher chance of trying cannabis; evidence that genes linked to trying cannabis go with schizophrenia was weaker. None of the gene studies looked at daily or strong cannabis. The researchers who did these studies, and experts reading them, disagree. See the contested question.
set.magnitude: Not estimable as a causal effect. Attenuation of the crude association by each cohort's adjustment: about 45% on average (10% to 80%; exposure contrasts not stated) (Moore et al., 2007). Co-relative (one registry study, misuse): OR 10.44 in the general population, 5.07 in full siblings, 3.52 or 3.92 in discordant identical twins (untested). Mendelian randomization, liability to ever use on schizophrenia: 1.04 (1.01–1.07) per doubling of the odds, MR-Egger 1.01 (0.93–1.10), 12 variants 1.03 (0.99–1.08) (Gage et al., 2017); 1.08 (1.02–1.14) per unit of log odds, rescaled 1.37 (1.09–1.67) ever vs never, 1.41 (1.09–1.83) adjusted for the variants' associations with ever smoking (Vaucher et al., 2018); per unit of log odds, 1.04 (p = 0.81) with 5 genome-wide significant variants, 1.10 (0.99–1.21) with 69 variants at p < 10^-5, GSMR after outlier filtering (74 variants) 1.21 (p = 0.017) (Pasman et al., 2018). Liability to schizophrenia on ever use: 1.10 (1.05–1.14) per doubling, MR-Egger 1.17 (0.96–1.43) (Gage et al., 2017); 1.16 (1.06–1.27) per unit, MR-Egger SIMEX 1.07 (p = 0.81) (Pasman et al., 2018). Genetic correlation rg 0.25 (SE 0.03).
set.exposure: Cannabis use (self-reported ever or frequent use; cannabis misuse in the co-relative study, a national registry study); in Mendelian randomization, genetic liability to having ever used cannabis
set.debate.evidence_yes: In seven general-population cohorts the association remained after each cohort's own adjustment for measured confounders (about 60 across the studies, among them other substance use, personality traits, intellectual ability and other mental health problems), was larger for each cohort's most frequent use (pooled odds ratio 2.09) than for ever use (1.41), and was found for psychotic disorder (2.58) as well as for symptoms; the review's authors read this as consistent with an increased risk independent of the confounders measured (Moore et al., 2007; see the answer on how often people use). Most of these cohorts excluded people with psychosis at the start; in the Swedish conscripts, counting only admissions at least five years after conscription gave similar results; in the Christchurch cohort, modelling suggested that cannabis predicted later symptoms rather than the reverse, and fixed-effects regression for unmeasured confounders that do not change over time made little difference (Moore et al., 2007). A cross-sectional sibling-pair study is also described as arguing against stable family confounding, and one review judged shared genetic effects unlikely to explain the association because schizophrenia risk variants explain little of the variation in cannabis use (Gage et al., 2016). The review by the group that produced the potency studies adds that the Dunedin association remained after adjustment for psychotic symptoms at age 11 and that in the Christchurch cohort people tended to use less once minor psychotic symptoms appeared, which argues against self-medication (as described by Murray et al., 2016). In the one co-relative study the odds ratio was still 3.52 (3.92 in the table) in identical twins discordant for misuse, which by the viewpoint's own criteria favours a partly causal over an entirely non-causal reading (Gillespie & Kendler, 2021). Genetic liability to ever using cannabis was associated with schizophrenia in the main analysis of two Mendelian randomization studies, at 1.08 (1.02 to 1.14) per unit of log odds, stable when any single variant was left out and after adjustment for the variants' associations with ever smoking, which its authors read as strongly supporting a causal role (Vaucher et al., 2018), and at 1.04 (1.01 to 1.07) per doubling (Gage et al., 2017), and in the third only by the outlier-filtered GSMR method with 74 variants (1.21, p = 0.017; Pasman et al., 2018). In the 11-site case-control study the odds rose from occasional to daily use and were highest for daily use of high-potency types (4.78 against 2.19 for daily use of low-potency types, although a difference between types was not statistically shown, interaction p = 0.25), and across 10 sites the incidence of psychotic disorder was higher where more controls used daily (r about 0.8) (Di Forti et al., 2019; see the answer on strong cannabis). As described in narrative reviews, high intravenous doses of THC can bring on brief psychotic symptoms in healthy volunteers (Murray et al., 2016; Gage et al., 2016; laboratory studies not read here), and two reviews judge the evidence strong enough for public-health messages that cannabis can increase the risk of psychotic disorders (Gage et al., 2016; Murray et al., 2016).
set.debate.evidence_no: Adjustment removed on average about 45% of the crude excess odds (10% to 80% by cohort, for exposure contrasts the review does not state), 60% to 80% in the three most comprehensively adjusted cohorts, and no study adjusted for all major confounders: early-life adversity and shared genetic effects were rarely measured (Moore et al., 2007; Gage et al., 2016; Hall & Degenhardt, 2009). Of the cohorts reported after 2007, the association did not survive adjustment in Zurich, and in ALSPAC it fell to the null after adjustment for tobacco and other illicit drug use (1.12, 0.76 to 1.65) (Gage et al., 2016). In the one co-relative study the odds ratio fell from 10.44 in the general population to 5.07 in full siblings and 3.52 in identical twins, a 66% decline that the viewpoint reads as familial confounding accounting for more than half of the association (Gillespie & Kendler, 2021). In Mendelian randomization the evidence ran more strongly the other way: genetic liability to schizophrenia was associated with ever using cannabis (1.10, 1.05 to 1.14, per doubling, p = 2.64×10^-5, Gage et al., 2017; 1.16, 1.06 to 1.27, per unit of log odds, with similar weighted-median and GSMR estimates, Pasman et al., 2018), and both teams read their results as weak evidence for an effect of cannabis use on schizophrenia and stronger evidence for the reverse, one suggesting that early symptoms or negative feelings might lead people at risk to use cannabis to cope (Gage et al., 2017; Pasman et al., 2018); the forward estimates shrank to 1.01 (0.93 to 1.10) by MR-Egger and 1.03 (0.99 to 1.08) with 12 variants (Gage et al., 2017) and were not significant with five genome-wide significant variants (1.04, p = 0.81; weighted median 0.95) or with 69 (1.10, 0.99 to 1.21) (Pasman et al., 2018). Lifetime cannabis use is genetically correlated with schizophrenia (0.25) and also with ever smoking, alcohol use, ADHD and risk-taking (Pasman et al., 2018). Specificity is doubtful: in one comparison of 9131 people with severe psychotic illness and 10,311 controls, daily tobacco smoking (odds ratio 5.11), recreational drug use (4.62) and heavy drinking (3.96) had odds ratios as large as cannabis use more than 21 times a year (3.47) (as reported by Ksir & Hart, 2016, without the adjustment set), and another review finds specificity of exposure in some studies but not all (Gage et al., 2016). The critical overview reads the family studies (most of the association disappearing after controlling for familial relationships in the Swedish registry; raised risk of schizophrenia in families of people with psychosis whether or not they used cannabis in a US family study) and the non-specificity as evidence of shared vulnerability, argues that a naturally occurring gradient of use carries a gradient of confounders, and concludes that "cannabis does not in itself cause a psychosis disorder" (Ksir & Hart, 2016). Rates of schizophrenia have not clearly followed rising cannabis use (see the answer on whether rates changed).
set.debate.neither_can_show: Cohort and case-control studies cannot rule out confounding by what they did not measure (family history, genetic liability, childhood adversity, premorbid functioning) or cannabis use that began during an unrecognized early phase of the illness, and adjusting for education or employment, which the illness itself may affect, can remove part of a real effect or add bias. Mendelian randomization protects against confounding by environmental and social factors that do not change genotype and, for the forward estimate, against reverse causation, but here its instruments index genetic liability to having ever tried cannabis and explain 0.15% to about 1% of its variation, so a small forward estimate says nothing about the risk with daily or high-potency use; the variants may act through traits such as impulsivity or risk-taking rather than through cannabis (only ever smoking was tested, in one study); the three studies draw on the same consortium data, with about 1500 people in both the exposure and the outcome samples of one; and the reverse estimate concerns genetic liability to schizophrenia, not diagnosed illness or its early symptoms, and assumes that schizophrenia risk variants act in the general population, most of whom never develop the illness (Gage et al., 2017). Weak instruments in two-sample designs bias estimates towards no effect, while overlapping samples bias them towards the observational association. A co-relative comparison removes family factors that relatives share but not those that differ between twins, and error in recording use weakens within-pair estimates more than population ones, so a decline with relatedness can overstate confounding; here it rests on one study whose twin estimate is printed two ways and was not tested. A genetic correlation above zero is expected under a causal effect as well as under confounding, so it cannot separate them on its own. Attributable fractions in these studies assume the associations are causal, and comparisons of rates across sites or over time are ecological.
set.debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). In the studies read, people who use cannabis, and especially those who use it often, are more likely to develop psychotic symptoms and disorders, and this is found in many independent cohorts. How much of that link cannabis itself causes is not known. A large part shrinks when measured differences between people are allowed for, and the one co-relative study and the genetic studies suggest that a further part reflects family background and shared genes, or genetic liability to schizophrenia making cannabis use more likely, so the evidence read here suggests the link is not wholly caused by cannabis. Whether part of it is, and how large that part is for daily or high-potency use, these designs cannot say: the identical-twin estimate stayed above 1 but was not tested, the forward genetic estimates are small, vary by method and concern only ever trying cannabis, and the case-control studies that show the largest associations with daily and high-potency use cannot rule out confounding or reverse causation. The critical reviews read here reach opposite conclusions (mostly shared vulnerability; partly causal) from overlapping evidence, the authors of the three genetic studies read their own results in different directions, and neither conclusion follows from these data alone.
set.grade.domains.risk_of_bias.note: Cohort and case-control estimates remain open to residual confounding (family history, genetic liability and childhood adversity were rarely measured) and to use during an unrecognized early phase of the illness (cards sc_moore_2007, sc_di_forti_2019, sc_di_forti_2015). Mendelian randomization is observational too: the genetic design addresses confounding by environmental and social factors and, for the forward estimate, reverse causation, but its instruments are weak (0.15% to about 1% of the variance in ever use), may reach schizophrenia through other paths (risk-taking and impulsivity; only ever smoking was tested, in one study) and come from overlapping samples (cards sc_gage_2017, sc_vaucher_2018, sc_pasman_2018: ROBINS-E high for the forward estimates; the reverse estimates, from instruments for schizophrenia liability, were judged some concerns on cards sc_gage_2017 and sc_pasman_2018). The sensitivity analyses reported (MR-Egger intercepts near zero but with little power, I² 67% in one study; similar weighted-median estimates; stable leave-one-out results; no change after adjusting for ever smoking) do not justify leaving confounding unrated.
set.grade.domains.publication_bias.note: Not assessable for the genetic studies; the cohort pools showed no small-study signal, with little power (card sc_moore_2007).
set.grade.reasoning: Observational evidence, Mendelian randomization included, starts low; down one each for risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness and imprecision, which is below the floor: very low. Counted once: the three Mendelian randomization studies share the International Cannabis Consortium exposure data (Pasman et al.'s genome-wide study includes it) and Psychiatric Genomics Consortium outcome data, so their agreement in the reverse direction is not independent replication; the co-relative figures are one registry study seen through a viewpoint by one of its authors, and the same study is read differently by Ksir & Hart (2016) and Gage et al. (2016); Hall & Degenhardt (2009) and Gage et al. (2016) restate Moore et al. (2007). A genome-wide association study shows genetic overlap, not cause; co-twin comparisons remove shared family factors, not others. The authors of the three genetic studies read their results in different directions, and the 2007 review read its cohorts as consistent with an increased risk; these readings are reported, not used as evidence. Status contested: credible evidence and credible critiques point both ways, so the six-part debate box applies.

evidence_set: Residual confounding would most likely inflate the estimates: studies adjusting for more confounders showed more attenuation, 60-80% of the unadjusted estimate in the 3 studies that adjusted most comprehensively, and few adjusted for early-life attachment, childhood maltreatment and trauma. Shared genetic effects are judged unlikely to explain the association because schizophrenia risk variants explain little of the variation in cannabis use; a cross-sectional sibling-pair study (association between duration of use and psychotic symptoms within sibling pairs) and fixed-effects regression in Christchurch argue against stable familial confounding; but a co-relative study found the association substantially smaller with closer genetic relatedness, suggesting that population studies overestimate it. No numbers are given for the genetic studies.

evidence_add.extracted: The authors read the evidence as consistent with the view that cannabis increases the risk of psychotic outcomes independently of confounding and transient intoxication, judge that further longitudinal studies are unlikely to resolve whether cannabis causes psychosis, and conclude that there is now sufficient evidence to warn young people that using cannabis could increase their risk of a psychotic illness later in life.

set.statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether rates of schizophrenia or psychosis changed as cannabis use rose: the studies that narrative reviews cite disagree, all are ecological, and their figures are second-hand here. As described in two reviews, an Australian modelling study by the reviewers' own group found no clear rise in psychosis incidence after steep rises in cannabis use in the 1980s and 1990s; a British modelling study judged it too early to see any rise in England and Wales; case-register studies in Britain and Switzerland (south-east London and Zurich) reported rising incidence of psychoses in recent birth cohorts; and a British study of people treated for schizophrenia in general practice found no increase, cited to a 2008 government advisory report (Hall & Degenhardt, 2009; Hall, 2015). Another review describes incidence of schizophrenia in south-east London as doubling between 1965 and 1999 while the share of patients who had used cannabis rose (Murray et al., 2016), and a third cites a 2009 paper on diagnosed schizophrenia in the UK from 1996 to 2005 among studies finding no change or a decrease (Gage et al., 2016). A critical overview states that UK cannabis use rose at least tenfold since the 1970s, citing a commentary for this, and that first admissions for schizophrenia did not rise and perhaps fell slightly, without a source for the admissions figures, and treats this as evidence against a causal effect (Ksir & Hart, 2016). Reviews that lean towards a causal reading call such evidence weak: it cannot show that the people who used cannabis are those who became ill, and it does not account for confounders or for other risk factors that may have fallen over the same period (Gage et al., 2016); even a causal effect would raise incidence only modestly, and changes in diagnostic criteria and services, poor administrative data and possible falls in incidence from social improvements could hide a rise (Hall, 2015). The 2007 systematic review cites the same Australian and British modelling studies rather than new data (Moore et al., 2007), and a 2021 viewpoint calls for controlled before-and-after comparisons where cannabis use rose after decriminalization (Gillespie & Kendler, 2021). Across places rather than over time, in one primary study of 10 sites in Europe and Brazil, adjusted incidence of psychotic disorder was higher where more controls reported daily use (r about 0.8) or high-potency use (about 0.7); this is an ecological correlation, and although the paper calls the two measures only modestly correlated (r = 0.2), its own site figures correlate at about 0.71 (editors' calculation), so the two correlations are not separate evidence (Di Forti et al., 2019). Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
set.plain: If cannabis causes psychosis, rates of schizophrenia might be expected to rise when more people use cannabis. The studies that reviews describe disagree: an Australian study found no clear rise after cannabis use went up, studies in south-east London and Zurich found psychosis becoming more common in people born more recently, and a review says that in the UK first hospital admissions for schizophrenia did not rise although cannabis use rose at least tenfold. These studies compare whole populations over time, so they cannot tell whether the people who used cannabis are the ones who became ill, and changes in how illness is diagnosed and recorded could hide a rise. They are known here only through reviews.
set.magnitude: No pooled estimate. As described in reviews: no clear rise in Australia (modelling); too early to detect in England and Wales (modelling); rising incidence in recent birth cohorts in south-east London and Zurich (case registers), with schizophrenia incidence in south-east London described as doubling between 1965 and 1999 (one review); no rise in a British general-practice study (cited to a 2008 government report) and no change or a decrease in diagnosed schizophrenia in the UK from 1996 to 2005 (a 2009 paper cited by another review); at least a tenfold rise in UK cannabis use since the 1970s (from a commentary) without a rise in first admissions (no source given). Across 10 sites: correlation of adjusted incidence with daily use among controls r = 0.8 (p = 0.0109) and with high-potency use r = 0.7 (p = 0.0286); the two exposures correlate across sites at about 0.71 by the editors' calculation from the site table, although the paper prints r = 0.2.
set.grade.domains.risk_of_bias.note: Ecological designs: modelling studies and treated or registered cases, which cannot link any person's use to their illness or account for confounders and other changing risk factors (Gage et al., 2016); the UK admissions figure has no stated source; the site comparison rests on 10 points and two strongly correlated exposures (card sc_di_forti_2019).
